# Welcome {-}

How many patients would you need to compare a new pain treatment with standard treatment? This tutorial helps you justify a sample size that can answer your research question, using clinical examples, calculations and simulation.

Although the examples are clinical, the principles of justifying assumptions, choosing a target difference, and examining power and precision also apply in psychology, education, and other quantitative disciplines [@lakens2022]. The tutorial is a suitable starting point for learning these principles and planning comparisons of two independent groups with a continuous or binary outcome, provided the calculation’s assumptions match your study. Later chapters introduce other planning goals and help you recognize when a different method is needed. For factorial experiments and repeated-measures ANOVA, including designs common in psychology, *[Power Analysis with Superpower](https://aaroncaldwell.us/SuperpowerBook/)* provides more directly applicable examples and simulations [@superpowerbook2022]. Studies involving multilevel models, prediction, or time-to-event outcomes need guidance matched to those analyses; [Other study goals and designs](#study-designs) points you toward relevant resources. What counts as a worthwhile difference should also reflect your field and research question.

## How to use this tutorial {-}

This tutorial is for students and researchers. Chapters 1–4 form the Core route for basic two-arm trial planning. Chapters 5–8 offer Advanced topics that you can consult according to your study question. The glossary and common questions are reference pages for either route.

Activities are learning exercises. Apps are the interactive software used in some activities, such as calculators, simulations and the report builder. Expandable misconception boxes explain common difficulties; the toolbar help explains the other reading features.

```{r tutorial-roadmap, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
roadmap <- paste(readLines("../figures/tutorial-roadmap.svg",
  encoding="UTF-8", warn=FALSE), collapse="\n")
# Numeric entities keep SVG text intact when R uses a non-UTF-8 locale.
roadmap <- paste(vapply(utf8ToInt(enc2utf8(roadmap)), function(cp) {
  if (cp > 127L) sprintf("&#%d;", cp) else intToUtf8(cp)
}, character(1)), collapse="")
cat('<figure class="tutorial-roadmap">',
    roadmap, '</figure>')
```

Each teaching chapter ends with an embedded *Check your understanding* quiz. The material comes together in a [cumulative quiz](#cumulative-quiz), with Core and Core + advanced routes.

You can open [the tutorial and an app together](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many), consult the [activity walkthroughs](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/activity-walkthroughs.html), or review terms in the [Glossary](#glossary). For your own project, [Other study goals and designs](#study-designs) helps you choose an approach. Its advanced section on [units of randomization, measurement, and analysis](#units-of-analysis) explains how grouping and paired measurements affect the information a study provides.

[Flashcards](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/flashcards/index.html) are available for Core and Core + Advanced, with a [question-and-answer preview](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/flashcards/cards.html) and Anki/Quizlet downloads. Questions and suggestions are welcome through [Feedback](https://forms.cloud.microsoft/e/j00AMibqi5).

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
## Core learning outcomes {#core-route .unnumbered .core-heading}

The linked sections should help you develop a sample size justification for a basic two-arm trial. By the end, you should be able to:

- [Define a clinical question and justify assumptions](#clinical-question), distinguishing the [expected difference](#expected-difference), [target difference](#target-difference) and [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold).
- [Explain Type I error probability, Type II error probability and power](#power), and [interpret results using a confidence interval](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically).
- Use [one simulated study and many studies](#activity-1-one-study-then-many) to distinguish [sample estimates](#sample-estimate) from [population parameters](#population-parameter) and see how results vary.
- [Calculate sample size for two proportions or two means](#calculations) and [adjust recruitment for expected losses](#account-for-expected-losses), distinguishing analyzable counts from recruitment counts.
- [Examine a plausible alternative assumption](#stress-test-the-study-plan), recognize [underpowered studies](#what-if-the-study-is-too-small-for-its-purpose) and assess [ways to increase power](#increase-power).
- [Write a short sample size justification](#write-a-sample-size-justification) recording assumptions, calculation and recruitment, using the [Activity: Develop and justify your study plan](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report).

:::

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
## Advanced learning outcomes {#advanced-route .unnumbered .advanced-heading}

The extensions below may be relevant to your study question. They should help you:

- Distinguish [an observed significance boundary from planned power](#critical-observed-difference) and explore [sampling distributions and error regions](#alpha-beta).
- [Read power curves](#curves) and evaluate what a fixed sample can establish.
- [Build a simulated clinical trial](#simulation) to examine power, coverage and precision, accounting for [Monte Carlo uncertainty](#monte-carlo-error).
- Plan a [two-group comparison for useful precision](#plan-for-precision) or a [single-population prevalence estimate](#prevalence), matching the criterion to the research question.
- Assess [existing-data reuse](#dataset-reuse), [rare-disease constraints](#rare-diseases), and the information needed for decisions in a [pilot or feasibility study](#pilot-feasibility).
- Recognize [study designs that need another method](#study-designs), including paired measurements and prediction models.
- [Reproduce calculations and simulations](#appendix) with their assumptions and methods documented.

:::


# Research question and planning assumptions {#clinical-question .core-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Explain why sample size starts with the clinical question.
- Identify the assumptions needed before calculating.
- Distinguish expected differences, target differences and clinical thresholds in a two-arm clinical trial.
:::

## The chronic pain study: how many patients do you need? {#the-chronic-pain-study-how-many-patients-do-we-need .core-heading}

Suppose you are planning a trial of a novel pain treatment against standard treatment. Does the novel treatment increase the percentage of patients reporting pain relief at four weeks?

You plan to randomly allocate patients to two [independent groups](#independent-groups) of equal size. The primary outcome is pain relief at four weeks: yes or no. A small pilot found relief in 7 of 10 patients receiving the novel treatment and 3 of 10 receiving standard treatment: 70% versus 30%, an observed difference of 40 [percentage points](#percentage-points).

Figure \@ref(fig:pain-pilot-patients) illustrates these pilot results.

```{r pain-pilot-patients, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.7, fig.cap="Illustration of the hypothetical pilot: ten patients per treatment group start with pain. Downward arrows lead to their outcomes at four weeks. Green figures with raised arms indicate reported pain relief; red figures indicate no reported relief at follow-up. The counts describe this small pilot sample.", fig.alt="Two treatment groups, each shown before treatment and after a downward arrow marking four weeks. All ten patients in each group start red, indicating pain. In the novel-treatment group, seven of ten become green with raised arms, indicating reported pain relief, and three remain red. In the standard-treatment group, three of ten become green and seven remain red: 70% versus 30% reporting relief."}
draw_pain_pilot_patients()
```

This looks promising, but twenty patients give you limited information. How many patients would make the main trial informative? In what follows, you will build a plan step by step, then examine what different repetitions of that study could show.

This first section focuses on two-arm randomized superiority trials: patients are assigned by chance to one of two treatment groups, and the aim is to investigate whether one treatment performs better than the other. Later chapters extend the reasoning to other outcomes, estimation, existing datasets and other study designs.

You can develop a study plan alongside the tutorial, beginning with the question and evidence. Your plan should include the calculation and recruitment target, and explain how uncertain assumptions affect the recommendation. The [Activity: Develop and justify your study plan](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report) brings these decisions together; you can develop the same report throughout the tutorial.

## What should this study establish? {.core-heading}

A sample size calculation helps assess what the planned study could establish under its assumptions. With too few patients, a study may miss a clinically worthwhile difference and produce a wide confidence interval. Recruiting more patients than the question requires also adds burden, time, and cost. For the pain trial, your plan should address four connected questions:

- Statistical: can the study detect a treatment benefit and estimate its size precisely enough?
- Clinical: how much additional pain relief would matter to patients?
- Ethical: does the information the study could provide justify participants' burden and risk?
- Practical: can you recruit the required patients within the available time and budget?

The final plan should address all four.

### Ethical review and the study protocol {.core-heading}

A scientifically sound study is an ethical requirement. The Declaration of Helsinki links reliable, valuable research to a justified protocol and prior [research ethics committee](#research-ethics-committee) review [@wmahelsinki2024]. Your protocol should explain the proposed sample size, the evidence behind its assumptions, and the information expected in relation to participants' burden and risk.

For clinical trials of medicines, ICH E9 provides a shared statistical framework used in Europe and the United States. Its sample-size guidance calls for an explicit outcome, target difference, analysis, error probabilities and assumptions, with sensitivity to uncertainty considered [@iche91998]. The statistical justification should follow your study question and planned analysis.

Review procedures depend on the country and study type:

- European Union: clinical trials of medicines within the scope of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 require scientific and ethical review; ethics committees operate under the law of the relevant member state [@ecethicsreview]. Other study types follow their applicable frameworks.
- United States: an [institutional review board (IRB)](#institutional-review-board) reviews studies subject to the relevant human-participant protections. FDA requirements apply to covered clinical investigations; HHS regulations apply to covered HHS-conducted or supported research [@fdairb2025; @hhsresearchreview].

Your institution's research office or ethics committee should help identify the applicable review route and protocol requirements. The Netherlands is one national example: research within the [WMO](#wmo) framework is reviewed by an accredited [METC](#metc) or the [CCMO](#ccmo), as applicable [@ccmowmo].

<details class="misconception" id="ethics-sample-size">
<summary>Why sample size is an ethical issue</summary>

A study should provide useful information in relation to the burdens and risks participants accept. An inadequate design may expose participants to those burdens without resolving its question; unnecessary recruitment adds avoidable burden. Scientific value, informed consent, fair recruitment, and the balance of potential benefits and harms all matter. A small feasibility study or rare-disease study may be ethically justified when its size supports a clearly defined objective. Its conclusions should match the information it can provide.

</details>

## What should you consider before calculating the sample size? {#how-do-you-determine-the-minimum-required-sample-size .core-heading}

Before choosing numerical parameters, you should consult guidance appropriate to the study design and research question. For a randomized trial, SPIRIT 2025 for the protocol and CONSORT 2025, together with relevant extensions, for reporting the results provide relevant guidance [@spiritconsort2025]. For other designs, you should consult the corresponding guidance, such as STROBE for observational studies or STARD for diagnostic accuracy; [Other study goals and designs](#study-designs) provides routes. These are reporting guidelines: they help identify decisions to document. Then you can specify the primary outcome, the expected results in each group, the planned analysis and the acceptable error probabilities. You can follow the question through to the analysis before choosing numbers [@fong2026; @wang2020]:

- Who are the patients, and how will treatment be allocated?
- What outcome will be measured, and at what time?
- What quantity will answer the question: here, the absolute difference in four-week relief percentages?
- Which analysis will estimate that quantity and test the hypothesis?

The map below gathers the remaining decisions. The chronic pain plan has two independent groups, equal allocation and a binary outcome. A different question or analysis may need a different sample size method.

You can begin your [study-plan report](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report) with the population, treatment comparison, outcome and assessment time. As you consider each question on the map, your report can record a provisional decision or what evidence is still needed. Later chapters supply the calculations and interpretation needed to complete it.

```{r study-questions-map, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
knitr::asis_output(render_question_map())
```

The examples use frequentist methods: two-sided significance tests for superiority and [confidence intervals](#confidence-interval) for estimation. [Estimation](#estimation) uses sample data to estimate a population quantity, such as a between-group difference. Precision describes how much uncertainty remains around that estimate, assessed here by interval width at a specified confidence level. A trial planned for power can also estimate the treatment difference; choosing a precision target changes how its sample size is determined. Non-inferiority, equivalence and clustered trials require different hypotheses or calculations; [Other study goals and designs](#study-designs) helps identify these designs. For Bayesian planning, see [@kunzmann2021review].

## What do you expect, what will you plan for, and what matters clinically? {#what-do-we-expect-what-will-we-plan-for-and-what-matters-clinically .core-heading}

In this tutorial, the [expected difference](#expected-difference), [target difference](#target-difference), and [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold) all refer to differences between treatment groups in the population of interest. They describe what you anticipate, what you use in the sample size calculation, and what additional benefit would be clinically worthwhile. Their values may coincide; the examples use different values to illustrate their roles. These group-level differences should not be interpreted as the benefit each individual patient would experience. See [Between-group differences and individual benefit](#between-group-differences).

Suppose the pilot and other relevant evidence support an expected difference of 40 percentage points. For the sample size calculation, the assumed target difference is 30 percentage points: 60% relief with the novel treatment versus 30% with standard treatment. Separately, after consulting with patients and clinicians, you set the minimally clinically relevant difference (i.e., the clinical threshold) at 20 percentage points.

The target difference is the assumed true between-group difference at which you evaluate [power](#statistical-power). Its choice should reflect evidence about plausible effects and judgments about clinical importance [@cook2018delta2; @cook2019delta2]:

- Relevant studies inform which between-group differences are plausible for this population and outcome.
- Patients and clinicians inform which benefits would matter in relation to harms and burden.
- The chosen target determines the difference at which you evaluate power.
- Calculations across plausible alternatives show how uncertain assumptions affect the required sample size.

The event probability here is the assumed probability of pain relief at four weeks. After observing a study, the percentage reporting relief estimates that probability.

| Quantity | Value | Role in this study |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Expected between-group difference | 40 percentage points | Best current expectation, with uncertainty |
| Target between-group difference | 30 percentage points: 60% versus 30% | Assumed true difference at which you evaluate power |
| Clinically worthwhile between-group difference (clinical threshold) | 20 percentage points | Smallest additional benefit judged worthwhile, considering burdens, risks, costs, and alternatives |

Table: (\#tab:pain-planning-values) Three distinct decisions for the chronic pain trial.

Figure \@ref(fig:planning-differences) places the three values in Table \@ref(tab:pain-planning-values) on the same scale. They answer different questions. The smaller target difference reflects uncertainty in this pilot estimate. Its choice requires justification from the available evidence. Your choice should be supported by relevant evidence and an examination of plausible alternatives. Absolute differences should be expressed in percentage points. A generic description of an effect as small, medium or large is insufficient justification [@caldwell2020].

```{r planning-differences, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Expected difference, target difference and clinical threshold for the hypothetical chronic pain trial. All three describe population differences between treatment groups, expressed in percentage points. Their values may coincide in other studies.", fig.alt="Three quantities on a common scale for novel minus standard treatment: the expected difference is 40 percentage points, the best current expectation; the target difference is 30 points, used to evaluate power; the clinical threshold is 20 points, the smallest benefit judged worthwhile."}
draw_planning_differences()
```

Choosing 30 rather than 20 percentage points has a consequence: a study planned for high power at 30 will generally have lower power at a 20-point benefit, even though that smaller benefit matters clinically. For this illustration, suppose the team considers a 30-point benefit realistic and large enough to support adopting the treatment. Its plan must acknowledge that a 20-point benefit could remain inconclusive. If reliably detecting the smallest worthwhile benefit is essential, evaluate the sample required at 20 instead. Affordability alone is not a justification for choosing a larger target [@cook2018delta2].

::: {.activity}
The plan uses a target difference of 30 percentage points. Under what circumstances would planning for 20 percentage points be more appropriate, and what would that change? Your explanation should consider patient and clinical judgments, the evidence, and the intended conclusion. These are hypothetical values; a real protocol needs outcome-specific evidence.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-target-choice">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A defensible choice in this illustration is a target difference of 30 percentage points, provided relevant evidence supports its realism and patients and clinicians consider that benefit worthwhile. The expected difference of 40 points is uncertain; it should not be used simply to obtain a smaller sample. The clinical threshold remains 20 points. Planning for 30 means accepting lower power at a worthwhile 20-point benefit. If reliably detecting that smallest worthwhile benefit is essential, 20 would be the appropriate target, with its larger sample requirement. More than one answer can be justified; the evidence, clinical judgment and intended conclusion should support the choice.

</details>
:::

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-pilot-effect">
<summary>Common misconception: the pilot reveals the true treatment effect</summary>

The pilot's observed relief percentages, 70% versus 30%, are [sample estimates](#sample-estimate) and could change in another small sample. They provide uncertain evidence about the population effect. The expected difference, target difference and clinical threshold answer different questions and should each be justified.

</details>

The pilot suggests a possible benefit, but its estimate is uncertain. It provides preliminary information for planning the study. After introducing error probabilities and power, you can [compare the pilot result with what a larger study could establish](#critical-observed-difference).

## Develop and justify your study plan {#record-assumptions .core-heading}

Your study-plan report develops alongside the tutorial. In this chapter, you can record the clinical question, effect scale and reasons for the three treatment differences. Chapter 2 informs the error probabilities and interpretation; Chapter 3 supplies the calculation; Chapter 4 adds expected losses, a simple sensitivity comparison and feasibility, then brings these decisions into a short justification. Unresolved entries can remain provisional.

When you revise an assumption, a short note about what changed and why will help you explain the final plan.

| Decision | What to make explicit |
|---|---|
| Research question: PICO | Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome, following @richardson1995; the outcome should include the measurement time point |
| Planning objective and constraints | Hypothesis testing with a power target, estimation with a precision target, both requirements, or a feasibility objective; whether the available sample is fixed |
| Effect scale | Treatment minus control; score units or percentage points; direction of benefit |
| Expected difference | Best current expectation, supporting evidence and uncertainty |
| Clinical threshold | Smallest benefit that matters to patients, with justification |
| Target difference | Difference used in the power calculation, with justification |
| Variation or event probabilities | Common standard deviation or control and treatment percentages; evidence source, population and time point |
| Sensitivity | Plausible alternative differences, standard deviations or event probabilities; identify the least certain assumptions |
| Analysis and power | Planned test and confidence interval; sidedness, Type I error probability and target power |
| Precision | Desired full confidence interval width and confidence level |
| Allocation and counts | Allocation ratio; per-group and total analyzable sample sizes |
| Recruitment | Expected losses, recruitment target, recruitment period and available resources |
| Intended conclusion | What the design could establish and what remains uncertain |

Table: (\#tab:planning-assumptions) Decisions and assumptions to record in a sample size plan.

PICO connects the clinical question to the calculation. In this example, its components are patients with chronic pain, the novel treatment, standard treatment, and pain relief at four weeks.

The target difference tells the calculation where to evaluate power. The [standard deviation](#standard-deviation) describes variation between individuals; the [standard error](#standard-error) describes [sampling variability](#sampling-variability) of an estimate. For binary outcomes, you should report each group's event probability as a percentage and their absolute difference in percentage points. The section [Glossary](#glossary) explains these terms in more detail.

For each numerical assumption, you should record the source, its relevance to these patients and this outcome, and a plausible range. Evidence from a different follow-up time or patient population may not transfer directly. For a clinical threshold, you should record the reasoning. DELTA² and CONSORT emphasize explaining the assumptions and calculation as opposed to reporting the final number [@cook2018delta2; @consortee2025].

A useful check is whether another researcher could reproduce your calculation from the description. In a review of 185 studies using the BREAST-Q Reconstruction Module, only 17 reported a sample-size calculation [@gallo2022]. This finding identifies incomplete reporting; the calculations and power of the remaining studies could not be assessed from that information. Your [assumptions report](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report) should make both the calculation and its justification traceable.

::: {.activity}
Which count belongs in the protocol: analyzable patients or patients to recruit? Your report should record both and explain the adjustment for expected losses when you complete the calculation.

You can develop your report in the [Activity: Develop and justify your study plan](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report). The text boxes let you build a study-plan report alongside your answers. Your clinical question and evidence come first; the sample size and recruitment counts can be added after the calculation activities. You can load a hypothetical two-arm example, save your entries, and download the report. Your report should clarify the role of the expected difference, target difference and clinical threshold, and explain what your study could establish.

This activity connects the numerical result to a defensible study decision. Your report should record the calculation or simulation results together with their method, inputs and interpretation.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-protocol-counts">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Your protocol should state both the required [analyzable sample](#analyzable-sample-size) and the number you plan to recruit, with per-group and total counts clearly identified. If 60 analyzable patients are required per group and 10% are expected to be lost, the recruitment target is ceiling(60/0.90) = 67 per group, or 134 in total. This allowance supports the expected analyzable count. Actual retention can vary, and missing outcomes require separate consideration in the analysis. The final report should use the count from your chosen calculation method and justify the assumed percentage lost.

</details>

:::


Small pilot effects are uncertain. Following up only pilots whose estimated effect gives an affordable main study can introduce additional bias [@albers2018]. A pilot can support conclusions about recruitment, acceptability, measurement procedures, and other feasibility objectives. It is generally not designed to establish treatment effectiveness, and its treatment-difference estimate may be highly uncertain [@eldridge2016]. In this tutorial, you examine plausible ranges explicitly; [further planning approaches](#further-planning-approaches) address more formal ways to account for uncertainty.

<details class="misconception" id="model-answer-pilot-threshold">
<summary>Common misconception: the clinical threshold should follow the pilot result</summary>

If the pilot had shown relief in 6 rather than 7 treated patients, should the clinical threshold change?

The clinical threshold should remain 20 percentage points. Changing one pilot outcome changes the observed treatment relief from 70% to 60%, and the observed difference from 40 to 30 percentage points, with standard treatment still at 30%. It may change your expectation of the treatment difference or your assessment of its uncertainty. It does not, by itself, change what patients and clinicians regard as a worthwhile benefit. The clinical threshold should reflect the benefit judged worthwhile by patients and clinicians.

</details>

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- A study plan starts with the clinical question, outcome, and analysis.
- Expected difference, target difference, and clinical threshold have different roles.
- The assumptions need evidence and a clinical justification.

</div>

# Understanding power and uncertainty {#power .core-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Explain [Type I error probability](#alpha), [Type II error probability](#beta) and [power](#statistical-power) under a specified population scenario.
- Distinguish [sample estimates](#sample-estimate) from [population parameters](#population-parameter), and the outcome of one study from the performance of a design across repeated studies.
- Interpret a confidence interval against zero and the between-group clinical threshold, and explain its repeated-study meaning.
:::

Suppose you repeated the same planned study many times, with the same sample size, analysis and specified true treatment effect. Power is the percentage of those studies that would reject the [null hypothesis](#null-hypothesis) given that the null hypothesis is false. At 90% power, about 90 out of 100 repetitions would detect that effect if it exists, while about 10 would not. This describes the design's long-run performance. You do not need to conduct the trial repeatedly: calculations or simulations estimate this probability under the stated assumptions.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-power-meaning">
<summary>Common misconception: 90% power means a 90% probability that the treatment works</summary>

Power assumes a particular true effect and describes how often the planned test would reject the null hypothesis across repeated studies. A study with 90% power can still produce an inconclusive result.

</details>

You can now return to the planning question: if pain relief is assumed to be 60% with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment, how often would studies of a given size detect the difference? Power describes this repeated-study performance under the specified assumptions.

## Hypotheses and error probabilities {.core-heading}

The null hypothesis says that the population pain-relief percentages are equal. Rejecting it means that the study provides sufficient statistical evidence of a difference, using the chosen test. When the test does not reject the null hypothesis, the evidence is insufficient to establish a difference. The confidence interval shows which treatment differences remain compatible with the data.

Let $\delta$ denote the population difference in percentages: novel treatment minus standard treatment. A positive difference favors the novel treatment; a negative difference favors standard treatment. The planned [two-sided test](#two-sided-test) asks whether this difference is zero or differs from zero in either direction. Here $H_0$ denotes the null hypothesis (no population difference), and $H_1$ denotes the alternative hypothesis (a population difference).

\begin{equation}
H_0: \delta=0, \qquad H_1: \delta\ne0.
(\#eq:hypotheses)
\end{equation}

For the sample size calculation, you assume 60% relief with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment—a true difference of 30 [percentage points](#percentage-points). Power describes how often the planned test would find a statistically significant result under that assumption. Power is calculated at the 30-point target difference. The statistical test assesses whether the population difference is zero.


```{r error-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Decision = c("Statistically significant difference (reject the null)", "No statistically significant difference (do not reject the null)"),
  `No population difference` = c("False positive (Type I error)", "True negative"),
  `Specified population difference exists` = c("True positive", "False negative (Type II error)"),
  check.names = FALSE), caption = "Testing decisions across repeated studies.")
```

A Type I error is a [false positive](#false-positive): rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true. The Type I error probability is the probability of falsely rejecting the null. In this trial, that means finding a statistically significant difference when the population relief probabilities are actually equal.

A Type II error is a [false negative](#false-negative): failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is false. The Type II error probability is the probability of missing a specified true difference. Power is the probability of detecting that difference: the true-positive probability, equal to 1 minus the Type II error probability.

For example, 90% power at a true 30-percentage-point difference means about 90 true positives and 10 false negatives per 100 repetitions of the planned trial. Here, positive means a statistically significant treatment difference, and negative means that the test did not find sufficient evidence of a difference.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-Type I error probability-meaning">
<summary>Common misconception: Type I error probability of 5% means a significant result has a 5% probability of being a false positive</summary>

If the treatments truly have equal population relief probabilities, a test with a 5% Type I error probability would give about 5 false positives per 100 repeated studies, under its assumptions. This is different from saying that 5% of all significant findings are false positives. That percentage also depends on how often real treatment differences exist and on the studies' power.

</details>

Type I error probability of 5% and power of 80% or 90% are common planning choices. Your choices should reflect the clinical question and the consequences of each error. Error probabilities describe how often each mistake occurs under specified assumptions. For the pain trial, a false positive could contribute to adopting an ineffective treatment that adds adverse effects or burden. A false negative could delay recognition of a worthwhile benefit. The consequences depend on the treatment and available alternatives. These considerations should inform the planned error probabilities, alongside relevant methodological and regulatory guidance. A non-significant result may reflect insufficient information to distinguish the treatments.

## Activity: Chronic pain: one study and many studies {#activity-1-one-study-then-many .core-heading}

The pilot found relief in 70% versus 30% of patients. For planning, you chose the smaller difference of 60% versus 30%. The simulation now asks what studies would show if those planning values were the true population probabilities. The 60% value defines the hypothetical population explored in this simulation.

In this simulation, the population event probabilities are specified as 30% pain relief with standard treatment and 60% with the novel treatment: a true population difference of 30 percentage points. Each simulated trial samples different patients, so its observed percentages and treatment difference vary.

### A couple of individual trials {.core-heading}

Before inspecting the results, which quantities would you expect to stay fixed and which would change across three trials? With 20 patients per group and the same population assumptions, the trials could give the following results:

```{r pain-sample-estimates}
example_trials <- lapply(20260941:20260943, function(trial_seed) {
  scenario <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = 20,
    p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
    seed = trial_seed)
  simulate_one_study(scenario)
})
trial_examples <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(example_trials), function(i) {
  trial <- example_trials[[i]]
  rates <- tapply(trial$data$outcome, trial$data$group, mean)
  data.frame(Trial = i, `Standard treatment: observed relief` = percent(rates["Control"]),
    `Novel treatment: observed relief` = percent(rates["Treatment"]),
    `Observed difference` = paste0(round(100 * trial$result$estimate), " percentage points"),
    `95% confidence interval` = paste0(round(100 * trial$result$lower), " to ", round(100 * trial$result$upper), " percentage points"),
    check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
knitr::kable(trial_examples, caption = "Three simulated trials with 20 patients per group, all sampled under the same 30% and 60% population event probabilities.")
```

The population assumptions stay the same across these trials. Their observed relief percentages, differences and [confidence intervals](#confidence-interval) do not. In a real trial, you observe the sample and estimate the population parameters; the simulation makes that distinction visible because its population parameters are known by construction.

### Clinical interpretation of a confidence interval {#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically .core-heading}

To interpret one trial, you can compare its confidence interval with both zero and the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold introduced for the chronic pain study. Zero represents no population difference; the clinical threshold represents the between-group benefit judged worthwhile in this example.

The estimated difference summarizes the treatment comparison. Its interval shows uncertainty around that estimate under the analysis assumptions. At the same confidence level, a narrower interval gives a more precise estimate. Three hypothetical 95% intervals illustrate the possible clinical conclusions:

```{r clinical-intervals, echo=FALSE}
clinical_intervals <- data.frame(
  lower_pp = c(2, -8, 22),
  upper_pp = c(28, 32, 42),
  interpretation = c(
    "Evidence of benefit; its clinical importance remains uncertain. The interval excludes zero and includes benefits below and above the 20-point threshold.",
    "An inconclusive comparison. Some harm, no difference, small benefits and clinically important benefits remain compatible with the data.",
    "The interval supports a benefit above the clinical threshold. All values in the interval exceed 20 percentage points, under the analysis assumptions."),
  plot_label = c("Benefit; clinical\nimportance uncertain",
    "Inconclusive\ncomparison", "Benefit above\nclinical threshold"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Interval for the difference in relief` = paste(clinical_intervals$lower_pp,
    "to", clinical_intervals$upper_pp, "percentage points"),
  `Clinical conclusion and explanation` = clinical_intervals$interpretation,
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Hypothetical 95% intervals for novel minus standard treatment, compared with zero and a 20-percentage-point clinical threshold.")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:clinical-interval-plot) places the intervals in Table \@ref(tab:clinical-intervals) on the same scale. Positive differences favor the novel treatment. You can see whether each interval crosses zero, crosses the clinical threshold, or lies entirely above it.

```{r clinical-interval-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Three hypothetical 95% confidence intervals on a common scale. The solid vertical line marks no between-group difference; the dashed line marks the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold. Each horizontal bar spans the stated interval limits.", fig.alt="Three horizontal confidence intervals for novel minus standard treatment. The interval from 2 to 28 percentage points excludes zero but crosses the clinical threshold of 20. The interval from minus 8 to 32 crosses both zero and 20. The interval from 22 to 42 lies entirely above 20."}
par(mar = c(5, 9.1, 4.3, 1), las = 1, bg = "white",
  fg = "#26343d", col.axis = "#26343d", col.lab = "#26343d")
plot(NA, xlim = c(-12, 48), ylim = c(.55, 3.55),
  xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i", axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
interval_rows <- 3:1
abline(h = interval_rows, col = "#e5e9ec", lwd = 1)
abline(v = 0, col = "#4b5560", lwd = 1.5)
abline(v = 20, col = "#72428b", lwd = 1.8, lty = 2)
axis(1, at = seq(-10, 40, 10), cex.axis = .95)
mtext("Difference in pain-relief percentages", side = 1, line = 2.4)
mtext("Novel minus standard treatment (percentage points)", side = 1,
  line = 3.6, cex = .85)
text(c(0, 20), 3.67, c("No difference\n0", "Clinical threshold\n20"),
  adj = c(.5, 0), cex = .85, xpd = NA)
text(-14, interval_rows, clinical_intervals$plot_label,
  adj = 1, cex = .9, xpd = NA)
segments(clinical_intervals$lower_pp, interval_rows,
  clinical_intervals$upper_pp, interval_rows,
  col = "#17658a", lwd = 3, lend = "butt")
for (limits in list(clinical_intervals$lower_pp, clinical_intervals$upper_pp)) {
  segments(limits, interval_rows - .09, limits, interval_rows + .09,
    col = "#17658a", lwd = 2)
  text(limits, interval_rows + .19, labels = limits, cex = .85)
}
```

For a 95% confidence interval and its corresponding two-sided test, an interval that excludes zero indicates statistical significance at the 5% level. Clinical interpretation also depends on whether the interval lies below, crosses, or lies entirely above the clinical threshold.

These intervals concern the population-level difference between groups; see [Between-group differences and individual benefit](#between-group-differences) for the implications for individual patients.

Across repeated studies, about 95% of intervals calculated with a 95% confidence-interval method would contain the true population difference, if the assumptions hold. The next part of the activity shows how repeated samples behave. Clinical interpretation also considers harms, burden, and the credibility of the study [@sandoval2025].

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-confidence-probability">
<summary>Common misconception: this interval has a 95% probability of containing the true difference</summary>

The true population difference is fixed, while the interval changes from sample to sample. The 95% describes how often the method produces an interval containing that difference across repeated studies.

</details>

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-power-precision">
<summary>Common misconception: high power guarantees clinically useful precision</summary>

A study can detect a difference from zero while leaving considerable uncertainty about whether the benefit is clinically worthwhile. Power concerns the testing decision; precision concerns the interval's width. You can consider both when deciding whether the study can answer the clinical question.

</details>

### Many trials and a larger sample {.core-heading}

Repeating the trial 5,000 times shows a range of possible sample differences. The larger samples generally give estimates closer to the specified population difference, although any individual trial can still differ from it.

```{r three-samples}
sample_sizes <- c(20, 50, 80)
batches <- lapply(sample_sizes, function(n) {
  scenario <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = n,
    p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
    width_target = .20, B = 5000, seed = 20260921 + n)
  simulate_trials(scenario)
})
power_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(batches, power_row))
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Patients per group` = power_results$n_per_group,
  `Statistically significant results` = percent(power_results$simulated_power),
  check.names = FALSE), caption = "Percentage of 5,000 simulated trials detecting the assumed 30-percentage-point population difference at each sample size.")
```

```{r sample-differences, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Observed treatment differences across 5,000 simulated trials at each sample size. The dashed line marks the specified population difference of 30 percentage points. Larger samples generally produce less variable estimates.", fig.alt="Three histograms of observed relief differences with 20, 50 and 80 patients per group, showing progressively narrower distributions around the same population difference of 30 percentage points."}
local({
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  for (batch in batches) {
    hist(100 * batch$results$estimate, breaks = seq(-100, 100, 5),
      xlim = c(-40, 90), col = "#b9d4f3", border = "white",
      main = paste(batch$spec$n, "patients per group"),
      xlab = "Observed difference in relief (percentage points)", ylab = "Number of trials")
    abline(v = 30, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#69509a")
  }
})
```

Figure \@ref(fig:sample-differences) shows [sampling variability](#sampling-variability); the table shows how often the planned test detects the specified population difference. The assumed true difference here equals the 30-point [target difference](#target-difference) used to evaluate power. The simulation uses the specified population probabilities of 30% and 60%.

::: {.activity}
<details class="activity-practice">
<summary>Practice with the activity, now or after this chapter</summary>

You can try [Activity: Chronic pain: one study and many studies](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many) with 20 patients per group, standard-treatment relief 30%, novel-treatment relief 60%, and Type I error probability 5%. One study, followed by another, lets you compare sample estimates with the specified population probabilities. For each interval, you can consider which differences remain compatible with the data relative to zero and the 20-point clinical threshold. Many studies shows the range of results and how often the test detects the difference. You can then compare 50 and 80 patients per group.

In this activity, *One study and many studies* brings both simulations together on one page. Simulate one study generates hypothetical patient outcomes. The animation connects the observed patient outcomes with the estimated between-group difference, then moves the pink estimate dot from the upper axis straight down to the same horizontal value on the lower axis. The lower plot accumulates the estimates from earlier trials. Each dot in the distribution represents one complete trial. *Animate 20 trials* builds a short sequence using fixed population probabilities; pause and replay let you follow the connection at your own pace. The reduced-motion option shows the same steps without moving dots. Further down the same page, Simulate many studies generates a larger batch of independent trials. The core task focuses on the distribution of estimated differences and the percentage of significant results; coverage and interval-width summaries are advanced extensions. After changing inputs, you should rerun the simulation: displayed results retain the assumptions under which they were generated.

</details>

Which quantities stay fixed across trials, and which change? Why does a larger sample give a more precise estimate, while more simulation repetitions do not increase the power of each trial?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-sample-versus-population">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Within a batch of trials, the specified population relief probabilities stay at 30% and 60%, so their true difference stays at 30 percentage points. The sample size, allocation, analysis, Type I error probability and clinical threshold also stay fixed. The patients sampled, observed relief counts and percentages, estimated difference, confidence interval, [p-value](#p-value) and testing decision can change from trial to trial.

A larger sample gives each trial more information, which generally reduces the sampling variability of its estimate and narrows its confidence interval. Increasing the sample size deliberately changes the design; it can also increase power at the same true effect. More simulation repetitions make the estimated percentage of significant results more stable. Each individual trial still has the same number of patients and the same power.

</details>

:::

This repeated-study approach follows the introductory teaching idea in @superpowerbook2022 and the use of simulation in health-sciences education [@thiesmeier2024; @rudolph2021]. The [advanced simulation explanation](#precision-of-a-simulation) examines how precisely a simulation estimates study performance.

The advanced chapter on [power and uncertain assumptions](#curves) explains the sampling-distribution diagrams and the pilot's significance boundary. The simple simulation here provides the background needed for the basic calculations.

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- Power is the probability of rejecting the null under a specified true difference.
- Different samples can give different results even under identical population assumptions.
- A confidence interval shows uncertainty in the between-group estimate and can be compared with zero and a justified clinical threshold.
- More patients and more simulation repetitions serve different purposes.

</div>

```{r quiz-power, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_chapter_quiz("power")
```

# Calculating sample size {#calculations .core-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Calculate approximate sample sizes for two independent proportions or means.
- Explain how the [target difference](#target-difference), variability, [Type I error probability](#alpha) and target [power](#statistical-power) affect the calculation.
- Distinguish per-group from total counts.
- In the advanced section, compare planning for target power with planning for a useful confidence-interval width.
:::

You can now apply these ideas to two-arm treatment comparisons. The formulas below assume two [independent groups](#independent-groups) with equal allocation and a [two-sided test](#two-sided-test). Studies that randomize hospitals, compare body sites within participants, or collect repeated measurements require calculations that account for dependence; see [units of randomization, measurement, and analysis](#units-of-analysis). The advanced section on [estimation with a precision target](#plan-for-precision) explains another way to plan the comparison. [Recruitment and feasibility](#feasibility) then considers whether you can obtain enough usable outcomes. [Other study goals and designs](#study-designs) introduces single-population estimation and other designs.

Having specified the chronic pain target difference and acceptable error risks, you can calculate the required number of analyzable patients. The first calculation concerns that trial; the next concerns a continuous-outcome comparison.

## How error probabilities and power affect sample size {#how-error-rates-and-power-affect-sample-size .core-heading}

Your sample size calculation needs to account for two choices: the acceptable Type I error probability and the target power. A lower Type I error probability requires stronger evidence before concluding that the treatments differ. Higher power means a greater probability of detecting the target difference if it is the true population difference. Both generally require more patients when the other assumptions remain unchanged.

For the normal-approximation formulas below, these choices are combined into a sample size multiplier, $M$:

\begin{equation}
M=\left(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta}\right)^2.
(\#eq:multiplier)
\end{equation}

Here, $\alpha$ is the Type I error probability, $\beta$ is the [Type II error probability](#beta), and $1-\beta$ is the target power. The two $z$-values translate these probabilities into positions on the standard normal distribution: the familiar bell-shaped curve, centered at zero with a standard deviation of one.

A [$z$-value](#z-value) describes how many standard deviations a position lies from the center of that curve. Its subscript gives the proportion of the distribution below that position. For example, $z_{0.975}=1.96$ means that 97.5% of the distribution lies below 1.96. This position is called a [quantile](#quantile).

For a two-sided Type I error probability of 5% and target power of 90%:

- The 5% error allowance is split between the two ends of the distribution: 2.5% in each tail. This gives $z_{1-0.05/2}=z_{0.975}\approx1.96$.
- The target power of 90% gives $z_{0.90}\approx1.28$.
- The multiplier is therefore approximately $(1.96+1.28)^2\approx10.51$, using the unrounded $z$-values.

This multiplier combines the chosen error probabilities and power. The sample size calculation also uses the target difference and variability. You can use the table below without calculating the $z$-values yourself. The appropriate calculation still depends on your study design and planned analysis [@kirkwood2003; @wang2020].

```{r multiplier}
alpha <- .05
target_power <- .90
M <- (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) + qnorm(target_power))^2
M
```

For a Type I error probability of 5% and target power of 90%, the multiplier is $M=$ `r round(M, 2)`.

```{r multiplier-table, echo=FALSE}
grid <- expand.grid(alpha = c(.05, .01), power = c(.80, .90, .95))
grid$multiplier <- with(grid, (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) + qnorm(power))^2)
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(grid, c("alpha", "power")), digits = 2,
  caption = "Normal-approximation sample-size multipliers for different Type I error probability and target-power choices.")
```

The [methods and software record](#tutorial-methods) identifies the procedures used here and explains what should accompany an exported calculation.

## Two proportions {.core-heading}

The event percentages in each group and the target difference between them are your starting inputs. For the chronic pain trial, the calculation assumes 60% relief with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment: a target difference of 30 [percentage points](#percentage-points).

For two independent groups of equal size and a two-sided test, the tutorial and apps use the normal approximation in R's `power.prop.test()` [@rcore]. You specify the two event probabilities, Type I error probability and target power. The result is the required analyzable number per group, before allowing for losses.

```{r proportions}
pi_t <- .60
pi_c <- .30
pain_plan <- power.prop.test(p1 = pi_t, p2 = pi_c,
  sig.level = .05, power = .90,
  alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
n_raw <- pain_plan$n
n_per_group <- ceiling(n_raw)
pain_lab_n <- n_per_group
c(per_group = n_per_group, total = 2 * n_per_group)
```

```{r proportions-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=n_per_group, `Analyzable total`=2*n_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Analyzable sample size for the chronic-pain trial using the normal planning approximation.")
```

The unrounded result is `r round(n_raw, 2)` patients per group. Rounding upward gives `r n_per_group` per group, or `r 2 * n_per_group` in total. This is the count used in the recruitment and fixed-sample sensitivity examples below. The `strict = TRUE` setting counts significant results in either direction for the two-sided test.

The calculation targets 90% power under the stated assumptions. Actual power for the planned test can differ because the calculation is approximate; simulation lets you examine that performance. Your report should identify the method, assumptions and rounding, and account for expected losses separately.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-definitive-sample">
<summary>Common misconception: the calculator provides one definitive minimum number</summary>

The calculated sample size depends on the effect, event probabilities or variability, error targets and analysis method you specify. It is a conditional planning result. You should check plausible alternative assumptions and whether the reported number is per group or for the whole study before interpreting it.

</details>

```{r proportion-changes}
proportion_cases <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Original", "Smaller difference", "Lower probabilities",
               "Type I error probability 1%", "Power 95%"),
  treatment = c(.60, .60, .30, .60, .60),
  control = c(.30, .45, .15, .30, .30),
  alpha = c(.05, .05, .05, .01, .05),
  power = c(.90, .90, .90, .90, .95))
proportion_cases$per_group <- mapply(sample_size_two_proportions,
  proportion_cases$treatment, proportion_cases$control,
  proportion_cases$alpha, proportion_cases$power)
proportion_cases$total <- 2 * proportion_cases$per_group
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(proportion_cases,
  c("treatment", "control", "alpha", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable sample sizes under alternative binary-outcome assumptions, using the same normal planning approximation as the tutorial and apps.")
```

For a yes/no outcome, the calculation uses the event percentage in each group. For example, 30% versus 15% and 60% versus 45% both differ by 15 percentage points, but they need not require the same sample size. The amount of [sampling variability](#sampling-variability) also depends on where those percentages lie. Halving the difference therefore does not necessarily multiply the required sample size by exactly four. The table lets you compare these assumptions directly.

Read a row as a conditional statement: if those event probabilities and that analysis are reasonable, then this is the approximate number required for the specified error targets. The smaller-difference row needs more participants because sampling variability makes that difference harder to distinguish from zero.

In [Activity: Two-proportion calculator](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/two_proportions/), you can first predict the change in required sample size when target power rises from 90% to 95%. Your comparison should keep both event percentages and the Type I error probability fixed. After checking the result, your explanation should relate the larger requirement to the higher probability of detecting the specified difference. It calculates an approximate sample size without generating patients. Its link to the reasoning lab carries that count across as a fixed analyzable sample, so you can simulate the planned test and compare its performance with the power target.

### Preventing gestational diabetes {#adherence .core-heading}

Suppose you want to find out whether probiotic supplementation prevents gestational diabetes in pregnant women with overweight or obesity (BMI at least 25 kg/m²). Randomly allocate women to probiotics or no probiotics, with otherwise comparable care, and assess gestational diabetes using a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Your plan should specify the supplement, diagnostic criteria and assessment time before planning. An assessment at 20–24 weeks needs justification against applicable clinical guidance: NICE generally recommends risk-based testing at 24–28 weeks [@nicegdm]. For an observational study of supplementation, confounding requires an appropriate analysis and planning method.

For this calculation only, assume gestational diabetes occurs in 20% without probiotics and is expected in 8% with probiotics: an expected reduction of 12 percentage points. You can choose a target reduction of 10 points, corresponding to 20% versus 10%, and a [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold) of 5 points. All these values are hypothetical teaching assumptions.

The same planning assumption can be expressed using either developing the disease or remaining free of it:

| Outcome entered | Without probiotics | With probiotics |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Develops gestational diabetes | 20% | 10% |
| Remains free of gestational diabetes | 80% | 90% |

Table: (\#tab:gdm-outcome-direction) Two ways to express the same assumed effect of probiotics.

The [lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=adherence) uses the second row so that a positive treatment-minus-control difference represents benefit. A 10-percentage-point increase in remaining disease-free is the same comparison as a 10-percentage-point reduction in developing the disease. Your report should state which event you entered and its direction; the clinical question remains prevention of gestational diabetes.

```{r adherence-case}
adherence_case <- teaching_case("adherence")
adherence_plan <- teaching_case_spec("adherence")
adherence_plan$n <- plan_n(adherence_plan, "testing",
  adherence_case$inputs$target_power)
c(analyzable_per_group = adherence_plan$n,
  recruit_per_group = adjust_for_dropout(adherence_plan$n,
    adherence_case$inputs$dropout),
  planning_power = spec_power(adherence_plan))
```

```{r adherence-case-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=adherence_plan$n, `Recruit per group`=adjust_for_dropout(adherence_plan$n,adherence_case$inputs$dropout), `Planning power`=percent(spec_power(adherence_plan)),check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Sample size and recruitment requirements for the hypothetical gestational-diabetes prevention trial.")
```

[Activity: Gestational-diabetes prevention trial](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=adherence). You can compare recruitment with a limit of 240 women and 15% expected loss per arm. With the planned sample fixed, you can then reduce the percentage remaining free of gestational diabetes with probiotics from 90% to 85%, while keeping the comparison at 80%. This corresponds to a smaller disease reduction, from 20% to 15%. Your explanation should address why power changes while the original recruitment plan and clinical threshold remain fixed.

The purpose is to test whether an apparently modest preventive benefit would require more recruitment than is available. The event in the app is remaining free of disease, so higher percentages are favorable. Under *Assumptions for the simulated studies*, *Custom effect or variability* changes the generating probabilities without recalculating the original plan. One study shows a possible result; many studies estimate how often the planned test detects the smaller benefit. Editing the planning probabilities recalculates the sample required for a revised plan.

Under these assumptions, the required recruitment total is `r 2 * adjust_for_dropout(adherence_plan$n, adherence_case$inputs$dropout)`, exceeding the proposed limit of 240. This is a reason to reconsider recruitment, collaboration or the study's aim. Increasing the assumed benefit merely to obtain a smaller n would not supply the missing evidence.

## Two means {.core-heading}

For a continuous outcome, you should identify the target difference and the [standard deviation](#standard-deviation) in the same measurement units before calculating.

In the formula below, $n$ is the number of patients needed in each group, $\delta$ is the target difference between the group means, and $\sigma$ is the assumed SD of individual scores within each group. The calculation assumes the same SD in both groups. The multiplier $M$ combines the error-probability and power choices explained above:

\begin{equation}
n\approx M\frac{2\sigma^2}{\delta^2}.
(\#eq:means)
\end{equation}

Suppose comparable evidence suggests a 4-unit [expected difference](#expected-difference) in a normally distributed improvement score. You can use a more conservative 3-unit target difference, with SD 5 in both groups, while patients and clinicians judge a 2-unit benefit clinically important. The example uses a hypothetical, approximately normally distributed improvement score. The Type I error probability is 5% and target power is 90%.

```{r means}
delta <- 3
sigma <- 5
n_per_group <- ceiling(M * 2 * sigma^2 / delta^2)
c(per_group = n_per_group, total = 2 * n_per_group)
```

```{r means-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=n_per_group, `Analyzable total`=2*n_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Approximate analyzable sample size for the continuous-outcome comparison.")
```

Using the multiplier of approximately 10.51, a target difference of 3 units, and an SD of 5 units:

\[
n\approx10.51\times\frac{2\times5^2}{3^2}\approx58.4.
\]

You therefore round upward to `r n_per_group` patients per group, or `r 2 * n_per_group` in total. Smaller differences are harder to distinguish from patient-to-patient variation and require larger samples.

<details>
<summary>Raw and standardized differences</summary>

The target difference of 3 score units is a raw between-group difference. Dividing it by the common SD gives the standardized difference: $d=3/5=0.60$. If the SD were 10 units, the same 3-unit difference would give $d=0.30$. The clinical difference is unchanged, but it is smaller relative to patient-to-patient variation and requires more patients to detect. A standardized effect is therefore not, by itself, a measure of clinical importance. Keeping the difference in the outcome's original units helps you explain what it would mean clinically; standardized measures can help compare results across scales [@kallogjeri2023].

</details>

<details>
<summary>Where does the assumed SD come from?</summary>

Previous studies can inform the SD, but their patients, measurement scale, follow-up time and analysis should be relevant to your study. The SD of change from baseline is not interchangeable with the SD of final scores. A review of knee osteoarthritis trials found substantial variation in pain-score variability across studies [@bentin2026]. Its estimates concern continuous WOMAC pain scores. The binary pain-relief example requires assumptions about event percentages.

Your study plan should identify the source of the assumed SD and explore a plausible range. Table \@ref(tab:mean-changes) shows what happens when the SD doubles; a published pooled SD should not be treated as a universal value for every pain study.

</details>

The simple formula helps explain how sample size depends on the target difference and variability. A calculation for the planned t test also accounts for the fact that the study must estimate variability from its patients. It therefore gives a slightly different sample size:

```{r t-test-planning}
t_plan <- power.t.test(delta = 3, sd = 5, sig.level = .05,
  power = .90, type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided",
  strict = TRUE)
t_plan
c(per_group = ceiling(t_plan$n), total = 2 * ceiling(t_plan$n))
```

```{r t-test-planning-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method=c("Normal approximation", "Planned two-sample t test"), `Analyzable per group`=c(n_per_group,ceiling(t_plan$n)), `Analyzable total`=2*c(n_per_group,ceiling(t_plan$n)), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Sample size requirements under two planning methods.")
```

For your protocol, you should use the calculation that matches the planned analysis. The two methods give different counts because they use different statistical approximations. You should round upward within each group before doubling the count; recruitment losses are considered separately.

Your study plan should record the input values, software or formula, whether the test is one-sided or two-sided, allocation and rounded counts.

<details class="advanced-explanation" id="gpower-assumptions">
<summary>Beware of your assumptions in G*Power</summary>

The continuous-outcome example above illustrates why you should understand each software input. The target difference between group means is 3 score units, the common within-group SD is 5, allocation is equal, the two-sided Type I error probability is 5%, and target power is 90%. The expected difference remains 4 units and the clinical threshold remains 2 units.

[G\*Power](https://www.psychologie.hhu.de/arbeitsgruppen/allgemeine-psychologie-und-arbeitspsychologie/gpower) asks for different effect-size measures depending on the selected analysis [@faul2007]. For an independent-samples t test, Cohen's $d$ expresses the target difference relative to the common within-group SD:

\[
d=\frac{3}{5}=0.60.
\]

The one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) procedure asks for Cohen's $f$. It describes the spread of the group means around their overall mean, relative to the within-group SD. With two equally sized groups, a common SD and no covariate adjustment, the group means each lie half the between-group difference from their overall mean. Consequently [@gpowermanual2023]:

\[
f=\frac{d}{2}=\frac{0.60}{2}=0.30.
\]

The letter beside the effect-size field changes which value you should enter. Table \@ref(tab:gpower-effect-sizes) shows the consequence of entering $d$ in a field that expects $f$.

```{r gpower-calculation}
gpower_d <- delta / sigma
gpower_f <- gpower_d / 2
anova_power <- function(n_per_group, f) {
  df_error <- 2 * n_per_group - 2
  pf(qf(1 - alpha, df1 = 1, df2 = df_error),
    df1 = 1, df2 = df_error, ncp = 2 * n_per_group * f^2,
    lower.tail = FALSE)
}
anova_n <- function(f) {
  candidates <- 2:1000
  candidates[which(anova_power(candidates, f) >= target_power)[1]]
}
gpower_correct_n <- anova_n(gpower_f)
gpower_wrong_n <- anova_n(gpower_d)
gpower_actual_power <- anova_power(gpower_wrong_n, gpower_f)
```

```{r gpower-effect-sizes, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Calculation = c("Two-sided independent-samples t test",
    "Equivalent two-group one-way ANOVA",
    "ANOVA with d mistakenly entered as f"),
  `Effect-size input` = c("Correct: d = 0.60", "Correct: f = 0.30",
    "Incorrect: f = 0.60"),
  `Analyzable per group` = c(ceiling(t_plan$n), gpower_correct_n,
    gpower_wrong_n), check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Required analyzable patients per group for a 3-unit target difference and SD 5: correctly specified effect sizes and a mistaken input. All calculations use a 5% Type I error probability, 90% target power and equal allocation.")
```

Entering $0.60$ in the $f$ field makes the software plan for a difference twice as large as intended: 6 units instead of 3. The resulting sample of `r gpower_wrong_n` patients per group would have approximately `r round(100 * gpower_actual_power)`% power to detect the intended 3-unit difference. The expected difference and clinical threshold are unchanged.

These counts were calculated in R using the corresponding noncentral t and F distributions and rounded upward to equal group sizes. They exclude recruitment losses. In G\*Power, the matching procedures are *Means: Difference between two independent means (two groups)* under *t tests*, and *ANOVA: Fixed effects, omnibus, one-way* under *F tests*. Both use an *A priori* calculation; the t test uses two tails and allocation ratio 1, while the ANOVA uses two groups.

Before using a result, you should check that the selected procedure matches the planned analysis and that each input has the meaning the software expects. Recording the target difference and SD in their original units makes the calculation easier to check. The [methods and software record](#tutorial-methods) explains what to retain.

For a planned analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), baseline adjustment introduces further assumptions about how the covariates relate to the outcome and how much variation remains after adjustment. The effect-size input should reflect that analysis. The simple $f=d/2$ conversion above applies to the stated unadjusted two-group comparison. The FDA's guidance discusses planning and prespecifying covariate adjustment [@fda2023covariates].

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why calculation methods can give different answers</summary>

The mean calculation here assumes the same population SD in both groups and plans a pooled two-sample t test. R's default `t.test()` uses Welch's method, which allows unequal variances; choosing that analysis needs matching planning assumptions. Similarly, continuity corrections or exact methods can change binary results. Matching methods matters more than forcing two calculators to display the same number [@rcore; @julious2023].

</details>

```{r mean-changes}
mean_cases <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Original", "Half the difference", "Twice the SD",
               "Type I error probability 1%", "Power 95%"),
  difference = c(3, 1.5, 3, 3, 3), sd = c(5, 5, 10, 5, 5),
  alpha = c(.05, .05, .05, .01, .05),
  power = c(.90, .90, .90, .90, .95))
mean_cases$per_group <- mapply(sample_size_two_means,
  mean_cases$difference, mean_cases$sd, mean_cases$alpha, mean_cases$power)
mean_cases$total <- 2 * mean_cases$per_group
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(mean_cases, c("alpha", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable sample sizes under alternative mean differences, variability and error targets, using the simple normal approximation.")
```

Before rounding, halving the difference or doubling the SD multiplies the required sample size by four. You can explain this relationship using equation \@ref(eq:means).

The [Activity: Two-mean calculator](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/two_means/) makes these relationships visible before you simulate any outcomes. Its normal approximation gives 59 analyzable patients per group for the example. The rehabilitation activity plans using a pooled two-sample t test, which accounts for estimating the common variance and can require a slightly larger sample. You can transfer the calculator's count to the lab as a fixed sample to investigate that difference.

### A rehabilitation case {#rehabilitation .core-heading}

The same calculation can compare two rehabilitation programs. Suppose the primary outcome is improvement at six weeks on a hypothetical continuous mobility score. The expected difference is 4 units, the target difference is 3 units, and patients and clinicians judge a 2-unit benefit clinically meaningful. The assumed common SD is 5 units. For this illustration, independent patients are randomized to the two programs and the improvement scores are approximately normal.

```{r rehabilitation-case}
rehabilitation_case <- teaching_case("rehabilitation")
rehabilitation_plan <- teaching_case_spec("rehabilitation")
rehabilitation_plan$n <- plan_n(rehabilitation_plan, "testing",
  rehabilitation_case$inputs$target_power)
c(analyzable_per_group = rehabilitation_plan$n,
  total = 2 * rehabilitation_plan$n,
  recruitment_total = 2 * adjust_for_dropout(rehabilitation_plan$n,
    rehabilitation_case$inputs$dropout))
```

```{r rehabilitation-case-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=rehabilitation_plan$n, `Analyzable total`=2*rehabilitation_plan$n, `Recruit total`=2*adjust_for_dropout(rehabilitation_plan$n, rehabilitation_case$inputs$dropout), check.names=FALSE), caption="Sample size and recruitment requirements for the rehabilitation comparison.")
```

[Activity: Rehabilitation: compare two means](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=rehabilitation). Before changing the SD from 5 to 7, how would you expect the required sample size to change? Your exploration should hold the target difference, error probabilities and analysis fixed. Greater individual variability makes the same mean difference harder to distinguish, so the plan needs more patients. You can then assess whether 10% expected loss and a recruitment limit of 200 make each plan feasible. You can compare the [confidence interval](#confidence-interval) with the 2-unit clinical threshold. Although an improvement score uses before/after information within each patient, this example analyzes one score per patient across two independent groups. A single-group paired comparison, repeated-measures model, or baseline-adjusted analysis needs its own planning method.

This activity connects the continuous-outcome calculation with a possible clinical interpretation. After reviewing the planned sample, *One study* generates independent, normally distributed improvement scores using the stated difference and SD. Its interval shows whether that particular simulated study is compatible with zero, the clinical threshold, or both. *Many studies* shows the range of possible conclusions under the same population assumptions.

The expected-loss adjustment gives a recruitment total of `r 2 * adjust_for_dropout(rehabilitation_plan$n, rehabilitation_case$inputs$dropout)`, below this example's cap of 200. Meeting the cap and power target still leaves questions about the credibility of the assumptions, measurement quality and the [precision](#precision) needed for a clinical decision.

## Discharge percentages {#discharge .core-heading}



Standard care discharges 80% of patients by a specified time point. Comparable evidence suggests an 18-percentage-point [expected difference](#expected-difference): 98% versus 80%. Patients judge an 8-percentage-point between-group benefit worthwhile. Those two values remain fixed while you compare the following sample size plans.

| Plan | Target difference | Target power |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A | A 20% relative increase from the 80% standard-care percentage | 80% |
| B | An absolute increase of 10 [percentage points](#percentage-points) | 80% |
| C | The same target difference as Plan A | 90% |

Table: (\#tab:discharge-task) Three discharge-study plans with a 5% Type I error probability and a two-sided comparison.

### Your task {.unnumbered}

Your answer should contain the treatment percentage for each plan, your prediction of which plan needs the most patients, the calculated per-group and total counts, and a short explanation of the differences. You can use [Two proportions](#two-proportions) or [Activity: Discharge percentages](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=discharge). Each calculated per-group count should be rounded upward to a whole patient before doubling for the two equal groups.

The expected difference remains 18 points and the clinical threshold remains 8 points throughout.

<details>
<summary>Show the calculation and interpretation</summary>

```{r discharge-answers}
discharge <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("20% relative increase", "10 percentage points", "Higher power"),
  control = .80, treatment = c(.80 * 1.20, .80 + .10, .80 * 1.20),
  power = c(.80, .80, .90))
discharge$per_group <- mapply(function(p, power) {
  sample_size_two_proportions(p, .80, alpha = .05, power = power)
}, discharge$treatment, discharge$power)
discharge$total <- 2 * discharge$per_group
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(discharge, c("control", "treatment", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable discharge-study sample sizes using the normal planning approximation in power.prop.test().")
```

The treatment percentages are 96%, 90% and 96%. The approximate totals are `r paste(discharge$total, collapse = ", ")`, respectively. Each per-group count is rounded up before doubling for the total. The expected difference remains 18 points and the [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold) remains 8 points in each comparison.

Figure \@ref(fig:discharge-grids) shows how the relative increase in Plans A and C and the absolute increase in Plan B translate into discharge percentages.

```{r discharge-grids, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.3, fig.cap="Discharge percentages in illustrative groups of 100 patients. A 20% relative increase from 80% gives 96%; an increase of 10 percentage points gives 90%. The grids display assumed percentages; the sample size calculation determines how many patients the study requires.", fig.alt="Three grids of 100 squares.
